title: The trial of the created Qur'an
word: The trial of the created Qur'an
hook: a question of theology becomes a test given by the state, and one scholar won't give the answer

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mu'tazilah, and your line: justice and reason. Did you look for a reason before a verdict? Yesterday's argument about the created Qur'an doesn't stay an argument. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

Questions of theology usually live in books and lecture halls. You can disagree about them over dinner and still pass the bread. For a stretch of time in the Abbasid caliphate, one question left the books and went to court. Judges and scholars were called in and asked, one by one: is the Qur'an created? There was a right answer, and the government had chosen it. Some said the words and went home. Some would not, and among them was a scholar in Baghdad, Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Today, the trial, and the man who stood still in the middle of it.
screen: `A QUESTION GOES TO COURT.` → `IS THE QUR'AN CREATED?` → `ONE SCHOLAR WON'T SAY IT.`

segments.voice: The episode has a name in Arabic: al-mihna, the trial, or the ordeal. It began with the caliph al-Ma'mun, who took up the Mu'tazili view that the Qur'an was created and ordered officials to test the scholars on it. Those who refused could lose their posts, or worse. The policy outlived him and carried on under the caliphs after him. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, the scholar whose name the Hanbali school carries, kept refusing. The accounts of his life, collected by his family and students, say he was held in chains, questioned, and beaten. And they give his answer again and again, in one shape: show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah of His Messenger, and I'll say it. The accounts also show what he did not do. He didn't call for a revolt. He didn't raise an army or curse the caliph from the pulpit. He just wouldn't say the sentence. Some of the reports say that afterward he forgave the men who had him beaten. In time a later caliph, al-Mutawakkil, ended the policy, and the trial was over. Two things came out of it. In Sunni theology, the position Ibn Hanbal held, that the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, became the standard position. And the scholars took a lesson about who settles questions of belief. A ruler had tried, with prisons and whips, and it hadn't worked. The state stepped in, and the state stepped back out. What stayed was a quiet man who kept asking for a verse.
screen: `AL-MIHNA: THE TRIAL.` · `A CALIPH CHOOSES THE ANSWER.` · `SHOW ME A VERSE.` · then, large: `THE STATE STEPPED BACK OUT.`

segments.voice: The practice: stand firm, gently. Settle, and breathe. Sit up a little straighter, the way you might in a hard meeting. Bring to mind one thing you hold to, something you'd quietly decline to say even if it would make life easier. Hold it. Now notice your jaw and your hands. Firmness doesn't need clenching. Let the shoulders drop and keep the conviction. Steady, not angry. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for steadiness. If you don't, just keep the posture: back straight, shoulders soft. The bell holds the time.
The trial of the created Qur'an. Al-mihna: when caliphs enforced the Mu'tazili view, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused to give the answer. Today's word.
screen: `THE TRIAL OF THE CREATED QUR'AN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the state stepped in. Today, if someone pushes you to say what you don't hold, ask, calmly, for their reason. Tomorrow, Imam al-Ash'ari. Day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the mihna as the time caliphs tried to enforce the doctrine of the created Qur'an, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal is honored, especially among Sunnis, for refusing under pressure.

fork.setup: you're Ahmad ibn Hanbal. officials of the caliph demand you say the Qur'an is created. what do you do?
options: say the words to get free.
denounce the caliph and call for revolt.
refuse calmly, and ask for a proof from the Qur'an or the sunnah.
fork.reveal: the accounts say he kept asking for a verse or a sunnah, bore prison and beating, and never called for rebellion.

original.note: Arabic: the trial, or ordeal; the name for this episode.

trapdoor: what you thought: an abstract argument scholars had in libraries.
what it means: a government test on whether the Qur'an is created, which Ahmad ibn Hanbal refused to pass.
what a scholar hears: al-mihna, and a lasting lesson about rulers trying to settle questions of belief.

sources.ref: Accounts of the mihna of Ahmad ibn Hanbal (e.g. Salih ibn Ahmad, Sirat al-Imam Ahmad; Hanbal ibn Ishaq, Dhikr mihnat al-Imam Ahmad)
sources.work: Early biographies of Ahmad ibn Hanbal

sources.ref: al-Tabari, Tarikh, on al-Ma'mun's letters ordering the test

notes: No dates given deliberately. Confirm the sequence: begun under al-Ma'mun, continued under his successors, ended by al-Mutawakkil.
'Held in chains, questioned, and beaten' and 'some reports say he later forgave those who had him beaten': confirm against the early biographies.
'Show me something from the Book of Allah or the sunnah' is a paraphrase of his reported reply, not a quotation.
'Became the standard position in Sunni theology': confirm wording; Twelver Shia and Ibadi views on the createdness of the Qur'an differ and are not discussed here.
Editor pass: hook no longer implies Ibn Hanbal was the only scholar to refuse; practice's closing line varied.
